title: India Overusing Powerful Antibiotics While Millions Lack Basic Medicines, Lancet Study Finds
excerpt: A first-of-its-kind global framework covering 186 countries reveals nearly all nations prescribe too many high-risk 'Watch' antibiotics. India's consumption is especially skewed, with broad-spectrum drugs dominating while essential first-line treatments remain underused.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 99% of 67 countries analyzed overuse WHO 'Watch' antibiotics, driving antimicrobial resistance.
  • India's antibiotic consumption is 18.3 DID per 1,000 people, exceeding the estimated need of 14.7 DID.
  • Only 27% of India's antibiotic use comes from first-line 'Access' drugs, significantly below the recommended level.
  • 80% of the world's need for specialized antibiotics is in lower-income countries, yet wealthier nations consume the most.

India is consuming far more broad-spectrum antibiotics than it needs while falling short on basic, first-line medicines, according to a landmark study published in The Lancet Public Health on 22 July 2026. The research provides the first scientific framework for estimating how much of each type of antibiotic a country should use based on its infection burden and resistance patterns.

A Framework for 186 Countries

Led by researchers at City St George's, University of London and the University of Oxford, the Wellcome Trust-funded study analysed antibiotic use across 186 countries, territories and areas — covering 99.8% of the global population. The team grouped nations into peer clusters based on poverty levels, infectious disease rates, antimicrobial resistance and healthcare system strength, then used the best performers in each cluster as benchmarks for optimal use.

They estimated that approximately 43 billion antibiotic treatment courses were needed worldwide in 2019, averaging roughly one course per person per year. About 77% of that total should come from the WHO's 'Access' group — everyday first-line treatments like amoxicillin that carry a lower resistance risk — suggesting the United Nations' 2024 target of 70% 'Access' antibiotic use by 2030 is achievable.

India's Antibiotic Imbalance

India's numbers tell a stark story. The study estimates the country needs 14.7 defined daily doses (DID) of antibiotics per 1,000 people per day — split across 7.8 DID of 'Access' drugs, 6 DID of 'Watch' drugs and 0.99 DID of 'Reserve' drugs. Actual consumption stands at 18.3 DID: 4.5 DID of 'Access,' 9.3 DID of 'Watch' and just 0.19 DID of 'Reserve' antibiotics.

Put plainly, India is using nearly double the recommended volume of 'Watch' antibiotics — medicines like ceftriaxone, azithromycin and ciprofloxacin meant for specific infections — while underusing both the cheaper first-line drugs and the last-resort treatments that patients with drug-resistant infections urgently need.

"Our study found that in India some patients were exposed unnecessarily to antibiotics while others did not have access to the right antibiotics to treat their infections."

— Prof Ramanan Laxminarayan, One Health Trust and Princeton University

A Global Pattern of Misuse

India is far from alone. Among 67 countries with available real-world data, 72% were using more antibiotics overall than estimated to be necessary. A striking 99% were overusing 'Watch' antibiotics, and 60% continued prescribing drugs the WHO considers should no longer be routinely used. Meanwhile, 42% of countries were underusing 'Access' antibiotics and more than half were not prescribing enough 'Reserve' drugs — leaving patients with life-threatening resistant infections without adequate treatment.

The study also exposes a global inequality: while higher-income countries currently consume the most 'Watch' and 'Reserve' antibiotics, more than 80% of the world's estimated need for these specialised medicines lies in lower-income countries, where infectious disease and resistance burdens are heaviest.

India's Prescribing Culture Under Scrutiny

The Lancet findings echo earlier domestic data. India's National Centre for Disease Control surveyed 20 tertiary care hospitals across 15 states in 2021–22 and found that nearly three out of four hospitalised patients were receiving antibiotics, with 57% of prescriptions for 'Watch' drugs. Only 6% of prescriptions were based on microbiological evidence — most antibiotics were started without culture confirmation.

Dr Kamini Walia, head of the Division of Descriptive Research at the Indian Council of Medical Research, pointed to unnecessary duplicate antibiotic coverage in Indian hospitals: 26.4% of prescriptions included duplicate gram-negative coverage, increasing costs and resistance risk without improving patient outcomes. She called for focused efforts to reduce unnecessary use of commonly prescribed 'Watch' antibiotics through better antimicrobial stewardship.

What Comes Next

The study's authors say their framework gives governments a practical tool to assess whether national antibiotic use patterns are broadly appropriate. Lead author Aislinn Cook of City St George's described a "double challenge" — reducing overuse of broad-spectrum drugs while expanding access for patients who still lack basic treatments.

For India — the world's largest consumer of antibiotics by volume — the implications are significant. Antimicrobial resistance already kills an estimated 1.27 million people globally each year, according to Lancet data, and India's combination of high infection burden, over-the-counter antibiotic availability and limited stewardship infrastructure makes it particularly vulnerable. The Independent Panel for Evidence for Action on AMR will now evaluate targets and policies to guide countries toward the study's benchmarks.

For the Indian diaspora, the findings underscore a concern many carry from home: the routine overprescribing of antibiotics in Indian healthcare settings, which affects not just those living in India but global resistance patterns that cross borders with travellers and trade.
